items.title: Ron Carter — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: So I'd played with Sonny Stitt as a single, for example

ctx.x: You were just beginning to tell us a little bit about the jazz scene in Rochester …

Yeah, I was in the house band of Joe Close, piano player who ultimately went to join Ernestine Anderson out in Seattle and Don Manning, the drummer. What we would do, we were the intermission band between the jazz acts that came in, and sometimes they would come as a single. So I'd played with Sonny Stitt as a single, for example, Slim Gaillard as a single, so I had a chance to get involved in that environment, learn some songs and watch guys do what they do,

you know. I met Sam Jones, met Ike Isaacs who was playing with Carmen McRae at the time, Teddy Kotick with Horace Silver at the time. So I had a chance to kind of look at what they were doing as well as listen. They assured me in New York, a good bass player can always find work. So, sounds like a plan. So I graduated from the Eastman School of Music in June of 1959 and moved to New York August that same year. When I got to New York and went down to Birdland as Chico was working, the cello player decided to stay…

items.title: Ron Carter interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 17, 1999
items.q: I remember Sonny Stitt as a sideman

ctx.x: How did your professors feel about that? Or wasn’t it even an issue for them?

Well most of them didn’t really care. I went to class on time and did the homework. Some of them didn’t care for that kind of music so they didn’t like what I did in classes, and the school did not encourage a jazz profile. And the strange thing is at that time there was the Eastman Theater, there was a show called “Jazz for Moderns” that would travel throughout the country. And they played at the Eastman Theater, it was a wonderful auditorium, it seated maybe 2,000 people. And they had great bands going all…
force in music, it’s hard to understand how a classical institution would continue to ignore its presence.
